planting.note: Fall-sow seed outdoors or cold-stratify 30 days; this deep-rooted species resents transplanting once established.

directions: Widespread across dry prairies, roadsides, and overgrazed rangeland of the central and southwestern United States, horsetail milkweed forms narrow whorled leaves on slender stems topped with flat clusters of small greenish-white flowers in mid-to-late summer. It is an important monarch host plant in arid regions where showier milkweeds struggle, tolerating heat, poor soil, and drought once its deep rhizomatous roots establish. Because foliage contains higher cardenolide concentrations than most milkweeds, it is best sited away from grazing livestock pastures. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining soil; established plants spread steadily by rhizome.

planting.note: Fall-sow with cold-moist stratification; this Great Basin species needs sharp drainage and resents wet winter soil.

directions: Native to dry sagebrush flats, pinyon-juniper woodland, and rocky slopes of the Great Basin, this low, sprawling milkweed forms broad rounded leaves pressed close to the ground beneath clusters of unusual pale cream-and-maroon flowers with inflated hooded crowns. It is a larval host for monarchs in high-desert regions where few other milkweeds persist, and its tuberous root allows it to survive extreme summer drought and cold winters. Specialty milkweed seed growers propagate it from wild-collected stock; seed benefits from a cold-moist stratification period before spring germination. Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil with full sun and minimal supplemental water once established.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed on the surface so winter cold and moisture trigger spring germination; plants go fully dormant by early summer.

directions: Found on open rocky slopes, sagebrush steppe, and the edges of ponderosa and oak woodlands from British Columbia south to California and east to the Rockies, this delicate saxifrage relative sends up slender flowering stalks bearing small white to pink star-shaped blooms in early spring. Like many western geophytic perennials it produces tiny bulblets along the stem and root crown, dies back completely by early summer drought, and reappears the following spring from its underground bulblet cluster. It is a larval host plant for several native moths and an early nectar source for small native bees. Plant in gritty, well-drained soil that stays dry through summer dormancy, mimicking the vernal-moist, summer-dry rock outcrops where it grows wild.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall; keep bone-dry through summer dormancy to prevent rot.

directions: Native to grassy openings, oak woodland edges, and coastal bluffs from Oregon through central California, Tolmie's star-tulip produces a single grass-like basal leaf and slender stems bearing pale lavender-white, densely hairy cup-shaped flowers in spring, giving rise to the common name pussy ears. Like other mariposa lilies it grows from a perennial corm that requires a completely dry summer dormancy to avoid rot, making it well suited to rock gardens and dry woodland margins rather than regularly irrigated beds. It is pollinated by native bees drawn to the fuzzy petal texture and provides early-season nectar in otherwise sparse spring woodland understories. Specialty native bulb nurseries sell dormant corms for fall planting; seed-grown plants take two to three years to reach flowering size.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in dappled shade; withhold water completely during summer dormancy.

directions: Found on shaded, brushy slopes and oak-chaparral woodland edges throughout the California Coast Ranges and Sierra foothills, this graceful mariposa lily sends up gently arching stems hung with translucent, pearly-white pendant globe-shaped flowers in late spring. The nodding lantern-like blooms distinguish it from the upright-flowered mariposa lilies and make it a favorite among rock garden and dry-shade native plant collectors. Its perennial corm demands a bone-dry summer rest period to avoid fungal rot, so it thrives best under the dappled light and summer drought of oak woodland rather than in irrigated garden beds. Native bulb specialists propagate it from wild seed collections, and it is slow but reliable once established in appropriate conditions.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in full sun to light shade; keep dry through summer dormancy.

directions: One of the most adaptable mariposa lilies, this California and Oregon native grows on open grassy slopes, foothill woodland edges, and clay-soil flats, producing large upright cream to white flowers marked with deep maroon blotches and purple tints at the petal base in late spring. It is considered one of the easier Calochortus species to cultivate, tolerating a range of soils including heavy clay as long as summer drainage keeps the dormant corm dry. The showy flowers attract native bees and are a highlight of California wildflower displays following wet winters. Grow from fall-planted dormant corms or stratified seed; established clumps slowly naturalize in dry, sunny meadow plantings.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall; requires sharp drainage and a dry summer rest.

directions: Native to dry grassy and chaparral-edge slopes of coastal and interior Southern California, splendid mariposa lily bears clear lavender-pink, bowl-shaped flowers with a darker purple basal blotch and a ring of fine hairs inside each petal, blooming amid the heat of late spring. It is well suited to Mediterranean-climate rock gardens and dry borders where its perennial corm can rest undisturbed and completely dry through the long summer. Native bees and small pollinating beetles visit the open, upward-facing blooms for pollen. Source bulbs from California native bulb specialists for fall planting, or sow stratified seed in containers kept dry over summer.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in fall in slow-draining clay or loam; keep dry through summer dormancy.

directions: One of the earliest mariposa lilies to bloom each year, this Southern California endemic emerges on grassy coastal sage scrub slopes and oak woodland clearings from Santa Barbara to San Diego, sending up pale cream to light pink flowers with deep maroon centers from March through May. Unlike many of its relatives it tolerates the heavier, slower-draining clay soils typical of its native grassland habitat, making it a good candidate for California meadow gardens. Its perennial corm requires a long, completely dry summer rest to survive, after which it reliably returns with the first autumn rains. The Theodore Payne Foundation and other Southern California native plant specialists propagate and sell it as dormant bulbs for fall planting.

planting.note: Plant dormant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall; summer-dry dormancy is essential once foliage fades.

directions: Common across open woodland, chaparral, and rocky slopes from Oregon through the California Sierra foothills, pretty face sends up a loose umbel of star-shaped golden-yellow flowers with a darker midvein on each petal atop a slender leafless stalk in late spring. Grass-like basal leaves appear with winter rains and wither as the corm shifts into dormancy ahead of summer drought, the hallmark pattern of California's geophytic wildflowers. Its nectar-rich flowers draw native bees and butterflies during a season when many other woodland bulbs have already finished blooming. It naturalizes readily once planted in well-drained soil that dries out completely over summer, pairing well with summer-dry companion grasses and shrubs.

planting.note: Plant dormant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall; blooms latest of the native brodiaeas, often into early summer.

directions: Found on grassy meadows, vernal pool margins, and open woodland clearings from British Columbia south through California, crown brodiaea produces a short cluster of deep violet-purple, funnel-shaped flowers held just above the grass on wiry stems, often blooming after most other spring geophytes have already faded, which gives it the common name harvest brodiaea. Its narrow basal leaves emerge with winter rain and die back completely as the corm enters dormancy through the dry summer months, a pattern typical of California's vernal bulb flora. The flowers are an important late-season nectar source for native bees and were historically harvested by indigenous peoples for their edible corms. It is easy to naturalize in a summer-dry meadow planting with well-drained soil and full sun.

planting.note: Plant dormant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall; tolerates more moisture and shade than most California geophytes.

directions: Native to grassy clearings and the edges of oak and conifer woodland from British Columbia through Northern California, forktooth ookow sends up a tight, congested umbel of deep purple-blue flowers atop a slender twining or upright stalk in mid-spring, with narrow grass-like leaves that wither as the corm goes dormant for summer. It is somewhat more shade- and moisture-tolerant than many of its California relatives, allowing it to persist at woodland margins rather than requiring full open grassland. The flowers attract native bees and butterflies, and the corms were traditionally gathered and eaten by Pacific Northwest indigenous communities. Plant dormant corms in fall for reliable spring bloom and allow the clump to naturalize undisturbed.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed or set out divisions; foliage dies back to a dormant rhizome through the dry summer.

directions: A fleeting but cherished sign of spring across California's coastal grasslands and oak-studded hillsides, this fragrant golden-yellow violet opens its brown-veined flowers from a spongy perennial rhizome beginning in late winter and fades underground by early summer drought. It is the primary host plant for the declining Callippe silverspot and other fritillary butterflies, making it an important restoration species for pollinator and butterfly gardens in Mediterranean-climate regions. Unlike woodland violets it prefers open, sunny grassland rather than shade, and tolerates the clay soils and summer drought typical of California prairie remnants. Grow from seed or nursery divisions planted in fall, and allow the foliage to die back naturally without summer irrigation.
